reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Advanced Pandas
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 11, Advanced Pandas. In the previous module, we worked with the basic building blocks of a DataFrame: selecting columns, filtering rows, sorting values, and creating simple summaries. Now we are going to connect those skills into larger, more realistic workflows.

The main idea is not to memorize a long list of Pandas functions. Instead, I want you to think about how a table changes from one step to the next. We may start with raw data, clean or transform it, reshape it when necessary, summarize it, check that our joins are correct, and then produce something that is ready for analysis or reporting.

[tts-break]

As you work through this module, keep asking yourself one question: what does this operation change in my data, and why do I need that change? That question will help you understand Pandas much better than memorizing syntax.

We will work with a small order dataset throughout the module so you can focus on the logic. By the end, you should be able to build a complete Pandas workflow that is readable, reusable, and easier to validate.

slides.title: From basic Pandas to advanced workflows
slides.transcript:
Think of Module 10 as learning individual Pandas tools, and Module 11 as learning how to combine those tools into a workflow.

For example, filtering a DataFrame is useful by itself. Grouping data is useful by itself. Creating a new column is also useful by itself. But in a real project, you usually do several of these things together. You might filter out records that do not belong in the analysis, create a new variable, group the rows by region, calculate summary measures, and then sort the final report.

[tts-break]

That is the transition we are making here. We are moving from isolated commands toward a sequence of steps that has a clear analytical purpose.

After this module, we will move into Module 12, Cleaning and Exploratory Data Analysis. The advanced Pandas techniques you learn here will be important there because cleaning and EDA often require several connected transformations rather than one single command.

slides.title: Our working dataset
slides.transcript:
We will reuse one small order dataset throughout many of the examples in this module. Keeping the dataset simple makes it easier to see what each Pandas operation is doing.

Each row represents an order. The order ID identifies the transaction. The date tells us when the order occurred. Region, channel, and category give us different ways to group the data, and amount is the numeric value that we will summarize.

[tts-break]

This is a useful structure because it resembles many real datasets. In a business setting, the rows could represent purchases. In healthcare, the rows might represent visits or claims. In education, they could represent course registrations or student activities. The Pandas techniques are the same even when the subject of the data changes.

As we continue, watch how the shape of this table changes. Sometimes we will keep the same number of rows and add information. Other times we will reduce the table into summaries or reshape it into a different format.

slides.title: Method chaining
slides.transcript:
Method chaining is a way to connect several DataFrame operations into one readable sequence.

Look at the code from top to bottom. We start with the orders DataFrame. Then we use query to keep only orders with an amount of at least seventy. After that, assign creates a new fee column, and sort values arranges the remaining rows from the largest amount to the smallest.

Before you run the code, try to predict which orders will remain and which one will appear first.

[tts-break]

When you are writing a chain, placing each method on a separate line inside parentheses makes the logic much easier to follow. It also makes debugging easier because you can identify the step that may be causing a problem.

Run the code in the browser and inspect the output. Then change the threshold from seventy to fifty and run it again. Notice how one small change near the beginning of the workflow changes everything that follows.

slides.title: query() and assign()
slides.transcript:
Two useful methods for readable workflows are query and assign.

Query is another way to filter rows. Instead of writing a Boolean expression inside square brackets, you can often write the condition as a readable expression. In this example, we keep Web orders with an amount of at least fifty.

Assign creates a new column and returns a new DataFrame, which makes it convenient inside a method chain. Here, we calculate a tax value based on the amount.

[tts-break]

These methods are not automatically better than every other Pandas style. The important goal is clarity. If regular bracket filtering is easier to understand for a particular condition, use it. If query makes the condition easier to read, use query.

Run the code and inspect the result. Then change Web to Store, or change the minimum amount. Small experiments like this are a good way to understand exactly how each condition affects the DataFrame.

slides.title: Named aggregation with groupby()
slides.transcript:
Grouping becomes much more useful when we calculate several summary measures at the same time.

Here, we group the orders by region. For each region, we calculate total sales, the average order amount, and the number of orders. Notice that we also give each output column a meaningful name.

This is called named aggregation, and it produces a report that is much easier to read than a table with vague or automatically generated column names.

[tts-break]

Think about how common this pattern is in real work. A department report might need total expenses, average transaction size, and the number of transactions. A healthcare report might need the number of visits, average length of stay, and total charges. A customer report might need total purchases, average purchase amount, and order count.

Run the example and compare the regions. Then try grouping by channel instead of region. The syntax stays almost the same, but the analytical question changes.

slides.title: agg() versus transform()
slides.transcript:
Aggregation and transformation can both be used with groups, but they return different kinds of results.

Agg reduces each group to one or more summary rows. If we group by region and calculate the average amount, the result is a smaller table with one average per region.

Transform works differently. It calculates a group statistic but returns a value for every original row. That means the number of rows stays the same.

[tts-break]

In the example, we calculate the average amount for each region and attach that regional average to every order. Then we calculate the difference between each individual order and its regional average.

This is very useful when you want to compare each record with its group. For example, you could compare each employee's salary with the average salary in the department, or each hospital visit with the average cost for that diagnosis group.

Run the code and pay attention to the row count. That is the key difference to remember.

slides.title: Pivot tables
slides.transcript:
A pivot table creates a cross-tab summary that is easy to compare.

In this example, region becomes the rows and channel becomes the columns. The amount column provides the values, and we sum those values for each region and channel combination.

The result looks more like a report than a raw DataFrame.

[tts-break]

Pivot tables are useful when people need to scan across categories quickly. For example, a manager may want to compare online, store, and email sales across several regions. A regular groupby can calculate the same information, but the pivot table may be easier to read.

Notice the fill value option in the code. If a region does not have a particular channel, Pandas can place a zero instead of leaving the cell empty.

Run the example, then try changing the aggregation function from sum to mean. The table layout stays the same, but the meaning of the values changes.

slides.title: Melt wide data into long data
slides.transcript:
Many datasets arrive in a wide format because that layout is easy for people to read in a spreadsheet.

Here, the months January, February, and March are separate columns. That may look convenient, but it can make grouping and plotting more difficult.

Melt converts those month columns into rows. After melting, we have one month column and one sales column.

[tts-break]

This is called long format, and long format is often better for analysis. It works naturally with grouping, plotting libraries, and many statistical tools.

A useful way to think about melt is this: the values that are currently stored in column names become values inside a new column.

Run the example and compare the number of rows before and after melting. Then imagine a spreadsheet with twelve month columns or fifty survey question columns. Melt can turn that wide structure into a much more analysis-friendly form.

slides.title: explode() for list-like data
slides.transcript:
Sometimes one DataFrame cell contains more than one value. For example, a customer may have several interests, a patient may have several diagnosis codes, or a document may have several tags.

The explode method turns those list-like values into separate rows.

In the example, Ava has two interests, Noah has one, and Mia has three. After exploding the interests column, each interest gets its own row while the customer name is repeated as needed.

[tts-break]

This structure is much easier to analyze. We can count interests, group by interest, or join the values with another table.

Run the example and look at the value counts at the bottom. Then add another interest to one customer and run the code again.

Explode is especially useful when data comes from JSON, APIs, or systems where one field can contain several items.

slides.title: Work with dates
slides.transcript:
Date columns often look like dates when we read a CSV file, but Pandas may still store them as text.

Before doing reliable time-based analysis, convert the column with pandas to datetime. Once the values are real datetime objects, the dt accessor gives us many useful features.

In the example, we create the weekday name and a monthly period from the date column.

[tts-break]

These features are useful because many analytical questions are based on time. We may want to compare weekdays and weekends, calculate monthly totals, study seasonal patterns, or filter records within a specific date range.

Always inspect the result after converting dates. Real-world date columns can contain missing values, inconsistent formats, or invalid dates.

Run the example and then try adding a year column or a numerical month column. The dt accessor gives you many options once the date has been converted correctly.

slides.title: Time-based summaries with resample()
slides.transcript:
Resample is designed for data that has a time component.

Instead of grouping by a regular category such as region or channel, resample groups observations into time intervals. Those intervals might be days, weeks, months, quarters, or years.

In the example, we convert the date column to datetime and then calculate daily sales totals.

[tts-break]

This pattern becomes very useful with transactional datasets. Imagine a table with hundreds of thousands of purchases. Looking at every transaction individually may not reveal a trend, but summarizing the data by week or month can make the pattern much easier to see.

Run the code using the daily frequency. Then change the frequency from D to W and compare the result.

The important concept is that resample changes the level of time detail. We are moving from individual observations to regular time-based summaries.

slides.title: Rolling summaries
slides.transcript:
Rolling calculations are useful when we want to understand short-term trends.

A rolling window looks at a group of nearby observations. In this example, the window size is three, so each rolling mean uses three consecutive sales values.

This creates a smoother series that can make patterns easier to see than the original daily values.

[tts-break]

You may notice missing values at the beginning of the rolling average. That happens because a three-row window needs three observations before a complete average can be calculated.

In some situations, you can change that behavior using the min periods argument, but first make sure you understand what the default result means.

Run the code and compare the original sales column with the rolling three-day average. Then change the window from three to five. A larger window usually produces a smoother trend, but it can also hide short-term changes.

slides.title: Create categories
slides.transcript:
Raw values are not always the form we want for analysis. Sometimes we need to convert them into meaningful categories.

Map is useful when you have a dictionary that connects one value to another. Replace is useful when you want to substitute selected values. Cut is useful when you want to turn a numeric variable into ranges.

In the example, we map Web and Email into an Online category, while Store becomes In person. We also use cut to classify order amounts as Small, Medium, or Large.

[tts-break]

These techniques are common in feature engineering and reporting. Age might become age groups. Income might become low, medium, and high. Product codes might become readable product names.

Run the code and inspect the categories. Then change one of the bin boundaries and see which orders move into a different group.

Always choose category boundaries carefully because those boundaries affect the interpretation of the analysis.

slides.title: Safer joins with merge()
slides.transcript:
A merge can run without an error and still produce the wrong analytical result.

That is why it is useful to validate the relationship between keys and inspect which rows matched.

In the example, orders are joined with customer information. The validate argument tells Pandas that many orders may belong to one customer. The indicator argument creates a column that tells us whether each row matched both tables or came from only one side.

[tts-break]

This kind of checking is important in real projects. A duplicated customer key could unexpectedly multiply rows. A missing key could cause information to disappear. Both problems may go unnoticed if we only look at whether the code ran successfully.

Run the merge and inspect the indicator column. Notice what happens to the order whose customer ID does not exist in the customer table.

A reliable analysis does not stop at merging. It checks the merge.

slides.title: Reusable workflows with pipe()
slides.transcript:
When the same transformation is used more than once, it is often a good idea to place that logic inside a function.

In the example, the add order size function receives a DataFrame, creates an order-size category, and returns the updated DataFrame.

Pipe lets us insert that function naturally into a Pandas method chain.

[tts-break]

This approach can make longer workflows easier to read and maintain. Instead of placing twenty operations in one large block, you can create several small functions with clear names.

For example, one function might clean column names, another might create categories, and another might calculate a report.

Run the code and follow how the DataFrame moves through the pipe function and then into sort values.

A useful rule is to keep each function focused on one clear responsibility. Small functions are easier to understand, reuse, and test.

slides.title: Mini workflow: raw orders to report
slides.transcript:
Now we can put several ideas together into one complete workflow.

We begin with the raw orders DataFrame. First, we convert the date column to a real datetime value. Then we keep valid positive amounts. Next, we create a monthly period, group by month and region, calculate total sales and order counts, and finally sort the results.

[tts-break]

This is closer to what Pandas work looks like in a real project. One function rarely solves the whole problem. Instead, we build a sequence of small transformations, with each step answering a specific question.

Before running the code, read the chain from top to bottom and explain what each line is doing in plain language.

Then run it and inspect the final report. If you can understand how the raw rows became the final summary, you are thinking about Pandas as a workflow rather than as a collection of unrelated commands.

slides.title: Practice challenge
slides.transcript:
Now it is your turn to build the workflow.

The starter DataFrame is already provided. Your task is to complete the missing Pandas steps.

First, convert the date column to datetime. Then keep orders with an amount of at least fifty. Create an order-size category using the ranges shown in the instructions. After that, group the data by region and calculate total sales, average order amount, and the number of orders.

[tts-break]

There is intentionally no completed solution on this slide. Use the earlier examples as patterns, but write the workflow yourself.

I recommend running your code after each major step instead of writing everything at once. For example, first confirm that the date conversion works. Then check the filtering. Then inspect the categories. Finally, build the grouped summary.

As an extension, sort the final table from the highest total sales to the lowest. The goal is not only to get an answer, but to build a workflow that you can explain.

slides.title: Module 11 wrap-up
slides.transcript:
You have now moved beyond basic DataFrame commands and into complete Pandas workflows.

We worked with method chaining, query and assign, named aggregation, transform, pivot tables, melt, explode, datetime operations, resampling, rolling calculations, category creation, safer merges, reusable functions, and pipe.

The common idea across all of these tools is that each operation changes the data for a reason. A strong Pandas workflow is readable, produces the shape you expect, and includes checks when something could go wrong.

[tts-break]

Before moving on, make sure you can explain the difference between aggregation and transformation, wide and long data, a regular groupby and a time-based resample, and a basic merge versus a validated merge.

In Module 12, we will use these Pandas skills for Cleaning and Exploratory Data Analysis. We will focus on missing values, duplicates, inconsistent data, unusual values, and patterns that deserve closer investigation.
